title: Using Ambient Scent to Enhance Well-Being in the Multisensory Built Environment
review_question: How does ambient scent influence well-being in the multisensory built environment, focusing primarily on indoor western urban developed spaces?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Anglophone literature focusing primarily on indoor western urban developed spaces.

synthesis_conclusions: Ambient smells in the built environment have a profound, often unrecognized, impact on mood, well-being, and behavior.
While malodors negatively impact well-being and can be linked to sick-building syndrome, pleasant ambient scents can positively influence mood, performance, and social behavior.
The effect of ambient scent is highly dependent on individual factors (liking, beliefs, associations) and context (intensity, natural vs. synthetic perception, prior conditioning).

Multisensory interactions are crucial; combining scents with other sensory cues (visual, auditory) does not guarantee positive outcomes and can lead to sensory overload or negative effects if incongruent.
Dynamic scenting, tailored to time and place, may be more effective than static scenting.
The field needs more long-term, ecologically valid studies in real-world built environments, considering the full multisensory atmosphere.
evidence_gaps: Lack of clear understanding of key factors determining when ambient scent effects occur.
Uncertainty about the long-lasting influence of multisensory cue combinations in the marketplace.
Limited research on how atmospheric/environmental multisensory cues interact to influence perception, behavior, mood, and well-being.
Need for more long-term studies in relevant built environments (offices, shops, home, transport) rather than laboratory studies with low ecological validity.
Need to learn more about how ambient smell interacts with other environmental sensory cues.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Many earlier studies on aromatherapy were statistically underpowered and not blinded, raising concerns about the robustness of reported results.
heterogeneity_sources: Contextual factors (intensity, natural vs. synthetic perception, prior conditioning)
Specific species of lavender used in studies

moderators.effect: Modulates the effect of ambient scent.
Determines the effect of specific odorants.

Women tend to be more influenced by ambient odors than men. Grapefruit scent had slightly more positive effect on males; rose scent had negative response for males (lower attention, higher anxiety, impaired mood).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Grapefruit scent had slightly more positive effect on males; rose scent had negative response for males (lower attention, higher anxiety, impaired mood).

moderators.effect: Congruent scent and music lead to more positive store environment ratings, higher approach/impulse buying, and satisfaction. Incongruent information leads to loss of processing fluency and negative valence.
Can lead to reduced positive outcomes (e.g., reduced unplanned purchases, negative response to increasing stimulus intensity).
Different scents may be appropriate for different locations (e.g., sleep-inducing vs. alerting scents).
Relevant for demonstrating effects of ambient fragrance.

limitations: The review is Anglophone, focusing primarily on indoor western urban developed spaces.
Many earlier studies on aromatherapy were statistically underpowered and not blinded, raising concerns about robustness.
Defining 'complexity' in the context of scents is difficult.
The effects of odors on the peripheral nervous system appear minimal and difficult to measure in normal subjects at rest.
It is unclear whether ambient atmospheric cues are automatically integrated in the same manner as cues belonging to the same object/event.
There is a danger that studying multisensory built environments may draw participants' attention to (in-)congruency, leading to artificial effects.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Odors directly access brain regions involved in emotion and memory, forming the biological basis for their affective impact.
The emotional and hedonic value of odors can be acquired through learned associations with experiences or environments.
The perception and impact of ambient scent on well-being are influenced by and interact with other sensory modalities in the built environment.

mechanism_chain.description: Proposed pathway for how ambient scent in the built environment influences mood and well-being, potentially interacting with other sensory inputs.

steps.from_construct: Ambient scent (e.g., pleasant, congruent with environment)

steps.to_construct: Activation of limbic system (e.g., amygdala, hippocampus) and associated cortical areas
Evocation of emotional responses (e.g., pleasure, relaxation) and/or retrieval of positive memories/associations
Improved subjective mood and enhanced overall well-being in the built environment
